what_it_does: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an AI technique where a language model, before generating an answer, first searches a large database of documents to find relevant passages to include in its context. The search step — finding the closest matching items in a huge library of numerical vectors (called embeddings, where each document is converted to a list of numbers that capture its meaning) — is called Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS). For very large databases this search requires reading enormous amounts of data from storage, and the bottleneck is moving that data from SSDs all the way to the CPU and back. REIS moves the ANNS computation inside the storage device itself — a technique called in-storage processing (ISP) — so the search happens where the data lives and only the small result set travels to the CPU. The authors redesign the ANNS algorithm to fit the internal structure of NAND flash controllers (the chips that manage SSD storage) without requiring major hardware changes to the SSD, and they also overlap the secondary step of actually retrieving the selected documents with the search computation to hide its latency.
